items.quote: Let’s go at once and report this to the royal palace.
items.contrast: Their earlier action of hiding goods versus their later plan to report the news.
items.reason: The earlier hiding is a plausible temporal misreading, but “after admitting wrong” points to the plan introduced by “Let’s go.” The stem and key clearly resolve the sequence.

items.quote: There was no one to rescue them because they lived a long way from Sidon and had no relationship with anyone else.
items.contrast: The circumstances preventing rescue versus the attack that created the need for rescue.
items.reason: The attack is a plausible general answer to why help was needed, but it does not explain why no help came. The explicit causal statement identifies distance and lack of relationships as the reasons.

items.quote: Now I know that the Lord will be good to me, since this Levite has become my priest.
items.contrast: The reason Micah states for his expectation versus an incidental fact about the Levite’s origin.
items.reason: Bethlehem is prominently mentioned and could be mistaken for the reason, but Micah’s statement introduced by “since” uniquely identifies the Levite becoming his priest as the cause.

items.quote: Listen to me, citizens of Shechem, so that God may listen to you.
items.contrast: The intended result of listening to Jotham versus an event within the story he begins telling.
items.reason: Anointing a king appears immediately afterward and is a plausible content-based distraction, but “so that” directly states the intended result: God may listen to the citizens.

items.quote: You mistake the shadows of the mountains for men.
items.contrast: Gaal’s identification of the shapes as people versus Zebul’s identification of them as mountain shadows.
items.reason: “People coming down” is plausible because Gaal repeats that claim, but the question asks for Zebul’s response to the first claim. Zebul clearly says the perceived figures are shadows rather than men.
